title: "What a boat does to the wind around it"
description: "Why can it be so hard to pass to windward, even when you normally sail higher and faster?"
date: 2026-10-26

[← All notes](../../index.qmd)

You are a little behind and to windward of a competitor on a beat. You normally sail higher and faster, but somehow you can't roll him. What is going on?

I looked for figures explaining this, but mostly found conceptual drawings without much data. A quick simulation seemed like a good idea. It turned out to be unnecessarily detailed, just like most other things I do.

## The simulation

I used [SU2](https://su2code.github.io/) for a 3D Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulation. The Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) equations describe the average flow, with an SST model accounting for turbulence. This gives a steady wind field around the boat.

The boat model was found online, with the sails adapted for this simulation. It is about 10 m long and 3 m wide, with a mainsail and jib.

<!-- Add the original boat-model credit and link when the source has been identified. Onsdagsbanen contains the simulation implementation, not the original attribution. -->

![The simplified hull, mast and curved sails.](boat-model.png){#fig-boat-model fig-alt="An oblique 3D view of a simplified hull and mast with a curved, twisted mainsail and jib."}

The boat sails at 6 knots in 5 m/s true wind at 10 m height, coming from 41 degrees to starboard. The hull stays upright and the sails hold their shape.

A logarithmic wind profile accounts for the sea's surface roughness: less wind near the water, more higher up. Combined with the boat's speed, this also changes the apparent wind angle up the rig. The sea is flat; there are no simulated waves.

### Getting the trim right

The first sails were too blunt. The final profiles have 8% camber, 0.1% thickness relative to chord, and separate trim and twist. I used 2D simulations at different heights to work on the trim, since a stalled sail would produce a very different wind field.

The 3D check below shows very little separation compared with what I would expect in real sailing. These sails are practically perfectly trimmed.

![Small regions of reverse flow: orange/red on the leeward side, blue on the windward side.](sail-flow.png){#fig-sail-flow fig-alt="A side view of transparent sails with narrow orange/red reverse-flow regions near their leading edges and upper mainsail, and a small blue region near the mainsail foot."}

### From 3D to 2D

The resulting wind field is hard to read. Overlapping surfaces obscure each other, making it difficult to judge what another boat would experience.

![Plenty of detail, but difficult to interpret. Red indicates worse estimated VMG; blue indicates better.](wind-3d.png){#fig-wind-3d fig-alt="The boat surrounded by overlapping translucent red and blue surfaces that obscure parts of the sails and wind field."}

To get one value at each position around the boat, I averaged over the sail height. A boat feels the disturbance across its whole rig, so each height is weighted by the combined local chord of the mainsail and jib. Heights with more sail area count more.

Wind-strength and direction contributions use the same area weighting and each layer's background reference. To combine them, I used a rough local approximation to a polar's effect on VMG:

$$
\Delta \mathrm{VMG} \approx 0.18\left(\Delta U - 0.18\,\Delta H\right)
$$

Here $\Delta U$ is the wind-speed change in knots and $\Delta H$ is the header in degrees; a lift is negative. The result is in knots of VMG. These coefficients are approximate, but let me compare both effects on one scale.

## Why passing to windward is hard

![The disturbance averaged over sail height. Red is worse, blue is better.](combined.svg){#fig-combined fig-alt="A boat pointing upwards, with a red wake trailing down and left, red shading to windward, and a blue patch ahead and to leeward."}

The long red wind shadow is familiar. But red also reaches around the windward side. Approaching from slightly behind, you can encounter **less wind and a header** before drawing level. Your usual advantage in clear air starts to disappear.

Now centre the same picture on your own boat. The competitor ahead and to leeward sits towards your blue patch: your disturbance can give them **more wind and a lift**. You may be helping the boat you are trying to pass.

### The two contributions

Both maps below use the same estimated VMG scale.

![The wind-strength contribution.](speed.svg){#fig-speed fig-alt="Weaker wind behind and to windward of the boat, with stronger wind ahead and to leeward."}

Less wind makes it harder to hold speed in the high lane. Bearing away to rebuild speed costs height.

![The wind-direction contribution.](direction.svg){#fig-direction fig-alt="A header behind and to windward of the boat, with a lift ahead and to leeward."}

The header makes that lane harder to hold, while the lift helps the boat ahead and to leeward.

If you have stopped gaining, pinching harder may just keep you in this relationship. **Tacking into clear air can be the better move**, giving you room to use your normal speed and pointing advantage again.

## About the result

The [Onsdagsbanen CFD code](https://github.com/chlyhne/Onsdagsbanen/tree/main/cfd) supplies the single-boat wind field. The two-boat explanation is a qualitative interpretation, not a simulated passing manoeuvre. VMG values are approximate, and the result remains exploratory because the background wind-profile check failed.
